title: Methodology — Vote-Scope
description: Explains how Vote-Scope projects seats: polls aggregated daily, Bayesian model, 10,000 simulations per riding. Transparent, independent, and continuously updated.
h1Html:
How we calculate
who's going to win
intro: Vote-Scope doesn't just display polls. It aggregates them, weights them, corrects for bias and simulates thousands of scenarios to produce a realistic projection — not a simple snapshot of a single poll.

sections.title: We collect every poll
sections.bodyHtml:
Every poll published by major firms (Léger, Abacus, Nanos, Mainstreet, EKOS, Angus Reid…) is entered with its date, sample size and polling firm. Recent polls count more — the model applies time decay.

For federal Canada: 190+ polls aggregated. For Quebec: 55+ provincial polls.

sections.title: We correct for firm biases
sections.bodyHtml: Some firms systematically overestimate a party, others underestimate it. We calculate these biases (house effects) from past election results and correct them automatically. The result: an estimate of true electoral support, not any one firm's bias.

sections.title: We estimate vote intention
sections.bodyHtml:
The model's core is a Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) — a statistical model that tracks vote intention over time while accounting for uncertainty. It generates a probability distribution for each party, not just a single number.

In plain terms: the model says “Liberals probably have between 44% and 50%” — not just “47%”.

sections.title: We simulate 10,000 seat scenarios
sections.bodyHtml:
For each simulation, we draw a plausible national result at random and apply it to each of the 343 federal ridings (or 125 Quebec constituencies, 124 Ontario ridings…). We account for the 2025 vote in each riding, regional dynamics and a local randomness factor.

The result: a realistic seat distribution — not a magic number, but a range with associated probabilities for each scenario.

sections.title: We publish and repeat tomorrow
sections.bodyHtml: Results are exported as static JSON and updated with each new run. The page shows the date of the last run. As election day approaches, recent polls carry more weight — and the range narrows.

callout: Key takeaway: Displayed seats are simulation averages, not a guaranteed prediction. A party projected at 218 seats could win 195 or 240 — the distribution shows this uncertainty. A 90% majority probability means in 9 out of 10 simulations that party gets a majority — not that it's certain.

cards.title: Where the numbers come from
itemsHtml: Public polls (Léger, Abacus, Nanos, Mainstreet, EKOS, Angus Reid, Pallas, Forum, Innovative…)
Geographic maps — Elections Canada, Census Bureau
By-elections, floor crossings and seat changes tracked manually

cards.title: What we don't capture well
itemsHtml: Strategic voting — hard to anticipate mechanically
Local star candidates who outperform their party
Very tight ridings — where the margin of error is greatest
Highly local sociolinguistic contexts (some bilingual, Indigenous ridings, etc.)

cards.title: No partisan affiliation
cards.bodyHtml:
Vote-Scope is a personal project by Kim Leclerc, journalist and data analyst. The model is not affiliated with any party, polling firm or media organization. It relies solely on public data and a transparent statistical methodology.

Methodological choices are documented here. If you spot an error or want to discuss the method, reach out via kimleclerc.ca.
